entry.title: Presentation at the 40th Interamerican Congress of Psychology

link.title: Presentation at the 40th Interamerican Congress of Psychology

entry.content:
This past July, I had the honor of participating in the 40th Interamerican Congress of Psychology (40CIP), held in the vibrant city of San Juan, Puerto Rico. Under the theme “A Psychology for all the Americas,” this event not only marked the Congress’s return to the “Island of Enchantment” after three decades, but also served as a fundamental epicenter for interdisciplinary exchange across our region.

Project Overview: Neurocomputational Profiling of C-PTSD

The project aims to move beyond symptomatic diagnosis by leveraging the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework, shifting the focus toward biological and behavioral mechanisms. By integrating computational modeling with traditional clinical measures, the team seeks to identify the “signatures” of trauma in women exposed to repetitive violence.

Key Components of the Research

Clinical Framework: The study distinguishes C-PTSD from traditional PTSD, focusing on the pervasive effects of chronic, repetitive trauma—such as domestic violence—on self-concept and affective regulation.

Methodological Innovation: The research employs a tripartite strategy:

Computational Modeling (Two-Bandit Task): Utilizes Reinforcement Learning algorithms to analyze decision-making processes under uncertainty.

Electrophysiology (Auditory Oddball Task): Uses ERPs (Event-Related Potentials) to capture neural responses to sensory stimuli.

Phenomenological Assessment (3D Body Image Scale): Explores the somatic and self-perception dimensions of trauma.

entry.title: Best Poster Price
entry.content:
I am honored and excited to share that I received the Best Poster Award at the Neuropsychoanalysis Association (NPSA) Congress held in New York this past June 2025.

It was an incredible experience to present our work on the integration of micro- and macro-process approaches to psychic change. Engaging with such a brilliant community of researchers and clinicians and receiving this recognition from the NPSA is truly a highlight of my academic career.

A special thank you to my colleagues and mentors who supported this research. I am looking forward to continuing our work in bridging the gap between clinical practice and neuroscientific perspectives.

entry.title: PUCP leads pioneering study on Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (C-PTSD) in female survivors of violence

link.title: PUCP leads pioneering study on Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (C-PTSD) in female survivors of violence

entry.content:
A research team at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú (PUCP) is leading a groundbreaking study to develop a neurocomputational profile for women exhibiting symptoms of Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (C-PTSD).

C-PTSD is a distinct diagnostic framework specifically associated with the experience of repetitive, prolonged traumatic events, such as domestic violence. Unlike traditional PTSD, this condition requires a more nuanced clinical understanding of how trauma reshapes long-term affective and cognitive functioning.

By utilizing a neurocomputational approach, our team aims to map the biological and cognitive signatures of this disorder. This research holds the potential to revolutionize our scientific understanding of the long-term impact of trauma on mental health and provides a critical foundation for designing more effective, evidence-based interventions tailored to the specific needs of women in Peru.

To learn more about the research I am currently conducting at PUCP, you can read the official article here: PUCP Research: Pioneering study on Complex PTSD
